title: Cushing Syndrome: Test When the Phenotype Fits
bottomLine: Evaluate Cushing syndrome when multiple progressive or discriminatory features make endogenous hypercortisolism plausible. Exogenous glucocorticoid exposure is the first cause to exclude; screening tests establish cortisol excess before localization.
recognize: Easy bruising, proximal weakness, wide violaceous striae, facial plethora, osteoporosis and difficult hypertension/diabetes are more discriminating than obesity alone.
Children may show growth deceleration with weight gain.
differentiate: Common obesity, depression and alcohol use can mimic portions of the phenotype.
Exogenous steroid exposure can come from oral, injected, inhaled, topical or unregulated products.
assessment: Review all steroid exposure and assess progression of discriminatory features, fractures, infection, diabetes, hypertension and thromboembolism risk.
workup: Use validated first-line cortisol screening tests and confirm abnormal results before localizing ACTH/adrenal/pituitary source.
Avoid random cortisol testing as a generic screen.
management: Refer confirmed endogenous hypercortisolism to endocrinology for etiologic treatment.
Taper chronic exogenous glucocorticoids safely when clinically possible rather than abruptly stopping.
medicationSafety: Abrupt cessation after prolonged glucocorticoid exposure can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Untreated hypercortisolism increases infection, osteoporosis, metabolic and thrombotic risk.
counselling: Explain why obesity alone is not enough reason for cortisol testing and why hidden steroid exposure matters.
followUp: Monitor metabolic, bone and cardiovascular complications during diagnostic/treatment planning.
examTrap: Ordering cortisol screening solely because a patient has obesity and hypertension.
oneLinePearl: Cushing testing needs a Cushing phenotype; first ask about steroids.

title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism: Confirm the Calcium-PTH Relationship
bottomLine: Primary hyperparathyroidism is hypercalcemia with an inappropriately elevated or nonsuppressed PTH after secondary causes and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia are considered. Management is driven by symptoms, kidney/bone involvement, age and guideline surgical criteria—not the PTH number alone.
recognize: Nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis/fracture, reduced kidney function and neurocognitive/GI symptoms can occur, though many patients are asymptomatic.
differentiate: Vitamin-D deficiency/CKD can cause secondary hyperparathyroidism without primary hypercalcemia.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia can mimic mild PHPT and usually should not be treated with parathyroid surgery.
assessment: Review stones, fractures, bone pain, kidney disease, medications such as thiazides/lithium, calcium/vitamin-D intake and family history.
workup: Confirm calcium and PTH relationship; assess renal function, phosphate, vitamin D, urinary calcium when appropriate and bone density/renal imaging for target-organ involvement.
management: Refer patients meeting surgical indications for parathyroid evaluation.
For nonsurgical management, maintain hydration and monitor calcium, kidney and bone outcomes rather than simply observing indefinitely.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary calcium/vitamin-D megadoses and review thiazide/lithium effects on calcium interpretation.
Severe hypercalcemia is an acute-care problem, not routine outpatient follow-up.
counselling: Explain why PTH can be 'normal' yet inappropriate when calcium is elevated.
followUp: Track calcium, renal function and bone density at clinically appropriate intervals.
examTrap: Calling a normal-range PTH reassuring when the calcium is high.
oneLinePearl: In hypercalcemia, PTH should be suppressed—'normal' can be abnormal.

title: Osteoporosis: Treat Fracture Risk, Not BMD Alone
bottomLine: Osteoporosis treatment is fracture-risk based. Prior fragility fracture, BMD, age and clinical risk determine treatment intensity; evaluate secondary causes, support exercise/nutrition/falls prevention, and match pharmacotherapy to fracture risk, renal function and long-term sequencing considerations.
recognize: Hip/vertebral and other fragility fractures can establish high fracture risk even when BMD is not dramatically low.
Vertebral fractures can be silent and present as height loss/kyphosis.
differentiate: Osteomalacia and CKD-mineral bone disorder require different treatment.
A low BMD result alone does not define the whole fracture-risk profile.
assessment: Review prior fracture, falls, family history, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, nutrition, renal disease and secondary endocrine/GI causes.
workup: Use fracture-risk assessment and DXA appropriately, with secondary-cause labs guided by phenotype.
Do not repeat BMD more often than the result can meaningfully change management.
management: Use Osteoporosis Canada guideline-directed antiresorptive or anabolic therapy based on fracture risk.
Plan duration/sequence from the beginning; denosumab discontinuation requires transition therapy to reduce rebound vertebral-fracture risk.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonate choice is affected by renal function/esophageal disease and rare atypical femoral fracture/ONJ risk.
Denosumab can cause hypocalcemia and must not simply be stopped without a follow-on plan.
redFlags: New thigh/groin pain on long-term antiresorptive therapy
counselling: Teach exercise/falls prevention and medication administration/adherence.
followUp: Track fractures, adherence, adverse effects and BMD only at intervals justified by treatment decisions.
examTrap: Stopping denosumab with no antiresorptive transition plan.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis care is fracture prevention—and every drug needs an exit strategy.

title: PCOS: Treat Reproductive and Metabolic Risk Together
bottomLine: PCOS is a diagnosis made after excluding important mimics. Management addresses menstrual/endometrial protection, hyperandrogenism, fertility goals and metabolic risk together; weight-neutral, non-stigmatizing care and screening for diabetes, lipids, BP, sleep apnea and mental health are central.
recognize: Irregular ovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology define the syndrome in the appropriate framework.
Insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk can occur at any body size.
differentiate: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumors are important mimics depending on presentation.
Rapid virilization or very high androgens is not typical uncomplicated PCOS.
assessment: Assess cycle pattern, hirsutism/acne, pregnancy goals, eating disorder symptoms, BP, diabetes risk, sleep apnea, mood and medication history.
workup: Exclude key mimics and assess metabolic risk with glucose testing, lipids and BP according to risk.
Ultrasound is not required in every patient when diagnostic criteria are otherwise satisfied.
management: Use combined hormonal contraception or cyclic progestin for cycle/endometrial protection when appropriate; use antiandrogen strategies with reliable contraception when indicated.
Metformin is useful for selected metabolic/glycemic indications and some reproductive contexts; fertility treatment follows ovulation goals/specialty guidance.
medicationSafety: Antiandrogens require pregnancy prevention because of fetal risk.
Avoid framing weight loss as a prerequisite to all care; use evidence-based obesity treatment when desired/indicated.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and discuss fertility without implying infertility is inevitable.
followUp: Track cycle control, metabolic risk, hyperandrogen symptoms and reproductive goals.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS solely from polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound.
oneLinePearl: PCOS is a reproductive-metabolic syndrome, not an ultrasound finding.

title: Lipid Disorders: Manage Absolute Cardiovascular and Pancreatitis Risk
bottomLine: Lipid management is risk-based. Separate secondary prevention/statin-indicated conditions from lower-risk primary prevention, identify severe hypertriglyceridemia and familial dyslipidemia, treat secondary causes and choose therapy according to absolute cardiovascular and pancreatitis risk rather than LDL alone.
recognize: Established ASCVD, diabetes, CKD and marked LDL elevation can create strong treatment indications.
Very high triglycerides raise pancreatitis concern and require a different immediate focus than modest LDL elevation.
differentiate: Familial hypercholesterolemia is suggested by very high LDL and premature family/personal ASCVD.
Secondary dyslipidemia can result from thyroid, diabetes, renal/liver disease, alcohol and medications.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, smoking, BP, diabetes, CKD, family history, pregnancy, alcohol, diet and medication contributors.
workup: Use fasting or nonfasting lipid testing as appropriate and investigate secondary causes when the pattern is severe/unexpected.
Use Canadian cardiovascular risk estimation when applicable.
management: Use statin therapy and nonstatin intensification according to risk/response/tolerance.
Address severe hypertriglyceridemia and reversible secondary causes promptly.
medicationSafety: Review statin interactions and investigate significant muscle/hepatic symptoms when indicated.
Pregnancy/planning pregnancy requires medication-specific lipid-therapy review.
counselling: Explain absolute-risk reduction rather than presenting LDL as a pass/fail number.
followUp: Repeat lipids after therapy changes to assess response/adherence and at appropriate long-term intervals.
examTrap: Withholding statin therapy in established ASCVD because the LDL is only mildly elevated.
oneLinePearl: Treat vascular risk first; the lipid number refines the plan.

title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy: Choose Treatment for Complications, Goals, and Safety
bottomLine: Obesity is a chronic disease and pharmacotherapy is selected for health complications, expected benefit, contraindications, pregnancy plans, adverse effects, cost/access and patient preference. Medication complements—not earns—behavioural support, and stopping effective therapy often leads to weight regain because the biology persists.
recognize: Complications include diabetes, OSA, hypertension, MASLD, osteoarthritis, infertility and cardiovascular risk.
BMI is a screening measure and does not capture all adiposity-related health impact.
differentiate: Rapid unexplained weight gain/loss or eating-disorder symptoms require a separate diagnostic pathway.
Weight-management medication for obesity differs from cosmetic/unregulated weight-loss products.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight; assess complications, eating disorder, medications promoting weight gain, pregnancy, gallbladder/pancreas history, mood and access/cost.
workup: Assess diabetes, BP, lipids, liver/sleep/other complications based on risk; avoid broad endocrine testing without clinical suspicion.
management: Use guideline-supported obesity pharmacotherapy when benefits fit risk/goals and continue effective therapy as chronic treatment when appropriate.
Consider metabolic/bariatric surgery pathways when indication/benefit aligns with patient goals.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy is a contraindication to weight-loss pharmacotherapy; medication-specific GI, gallbladder, cardiovascular, psychiatric and interaction risks require review.
Avoid compounded/unregulated products when approved therapy is intended.
counselling: Use person-first non-stigmatizing language and set health/function goals beyond kilograms.
followUp: Track tolerability, complications, function and meaningful treatment response; change strategy if ineffective or unsafe.
examTrap: Requiring a patient to 'fail lifestyle' before discussing evidence-based obesity medication.
oneLinePearl: Obesity medication is chronic-disease therapy, not a reward for weight-loss effort.

title: Sodium and Potassium Disorders: Symptoms, ECG, and Rate of Change Drive Urgency
bottomLine: Electrolyte emergencies are not managed from the number alone. Sodium treatment depends on tonicity, symptoms, chronicity and cause; potassium treatment depends on ECG/neuromuscular risk, severity, renal function and ongoing shift/loss. Stabilize dangerous physiology first, then correct the cause at a safe rate.
recognize: Severe hyponatremia can cause seizure/encephalopathy; overly rapid chronic correction risks osmotic demyelination.
Hyperkalemia can cause lethal conduction abnormalities even before symptoms, while hypokalemia can provoke weakness and arrhythmia.
differentiate: Pseudohyponatremia/translocational hyponatremia differ from true hypotonic hyponatremia.
Hemolyzed specimens can create pseudohyperkalemia and should be reconciled with ECG/clinical context when safe.
assessment: Assess neurologic symptoms, volume status, ECG, renal function, medications/diuretics/RAAS drugs, GI losses, endocrine disease and rate of change.
workup: For sodium, establish serum osmolality and urine studies/volume context when appropriate.
For potassium, confirm unexpected results and assess ECG/renal/acid-base context.
management: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia requires monitored hypertonic-saline strategy with correction limits and frequent sodium checks.
Dangerous hyperkalemia management separates membrane stabilization, intracellular shift and potassium removal.
Correct magnesium when relevant to refractory potassium disturbance.
medicationSafety: Do not correct chronic sodium disorders rapidly.
Insulin for hyperkalemia can cause hypoglycemia; monitor glucose.
RAAS blockers/spironolactone, diuretics and supplements can drive recurrence.
counselling: Review medication/supplement contributors and give recurrence precautions.
followUp: Trend electrolyte response after interventions and reassess underlying cause.
examTrap: Choosing a treatment from the electrolyte number before assessing symptoms, ECG and chronicity.
oneLinePearl: Electrolyte urgency is number + symptoms + ECG + rate of change.

title: Calcium Disorders: Confirm True Calcium, Then Treat the Physiology
bottomLine: Confirm that calcium abnormality is physiologically real using albumin context or ionized calcium when appropriate, then use PTH to divide the differential. Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia or hypocalcemia is an acute-care problem; chronic management targets the cause and prevents renal, cardiac and skeletal complications.
recognize: Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration, polyuria, constipation, confusion and arrhythmia; hypocalcemia can cause paresthesia, tetany, seizure and QT prolongation.
Albumin changes alter total calcium without necessarily changing ionized calcium.
differentiate: High calcium with nonsuppressed PTH suggests PTH-mediated disease; suppressed PTH points toward malignancy, vitamin-D/granulomatous or other causes.
Hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism differs from vitamin-D deficiency/CKD/magnesium-driven disease.
assessment: Review symptoms, hydration, stones, fractures, malignancy, surgery, kidney disease, supplements and medications such as thiazides/lithium/bisphosphonate/denosumab.
workup: Confirm corrected/ionized calcium as appropriate and obtain PTH, phosphate, magnesium, renal function and cause-directed vitamin-D/malignancy testing.
management: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires IV fluid-based acute management plus cause-specific therapy.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium and magnesium correction when needed.
Chronic care treats the underlying endocrine/renal/nutritional cause.
medicationSafety: Overaggressive calcium/vitamin-D replacement can cause hypercalciuria/renal injury.
Antiresorptive therapy can precipitate hypocalcemia in high-risk patients if calcium/vitamin-D status is not addressed.
counselling: Explain that total calcium can be misleading when albumin is abnormal and that the cause determines long-term treatment.
followUp: Trend calcium, renal function and cause-specific markers after treatment.
examTrap: Treating a low total calcium as true hypocalcemia without considering albumin/ionized calcium context.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the calcium, check the PTH, then treat the mechanism.
